content.title: About
content.content: Mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of various fungi that are consumed as food. They have a mild, slightly earthy flavor and a range of textures from tender to firm. Mushrooms are cultivated in controlled environments and harvested from the wild, and they are used in soups, sauces, salads, and as a standalone dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms belong to their own kingdom – Fungi – and are neither plants nor animals.
The largest living organism on Earth is the Armillaria ostoyae fungus in Oregon, covering over 2,000 hectares.
Certain mushroom species, such as button mushrooms, can be grown year‑round in fully controlled indoor farms.
Mushrooms play a crucial role in ecosystems by decomposing wood and other organic matter.
In Japan, mushroom‑derived enzymes (myco‑enzymes) are popular in traditional medicine.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide niacin, riboflavin, thiamine and, in some varieties, vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: A 100 g serving of mushrooms contains about 3 g of protein with very few calories, making them a good meat alternative.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Ergothioneine and selenium in mushrooms help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Beta‑glucans in mushroom cell walls stimulate the body's immune response.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in mushrooms aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Toxic wild varieties
items.content: Certain wild mushrooms are poisonous; collecting them without expert knowledge can lead to severe poisoning.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms are relatively high in purines, which may be a concern for people with gout.

items.title: Mold and mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improper storage can allow mold growth and the formation of mycotoxins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mushrooms can be eaten raw in salads, sautéed, stewed, baked, or boiled. They are commonly added to sauces, stews, pizza, and omelets. Before cooking, gently clean the caps to remove dirt and discard tough stems if present.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh mushrooms in a paper bag in the refrigerator for 1–3 days. For longer storage, blanch and freeze them or dry them in a low‑heat oven.
